guards.rule: A cushion placed on a bed must sit on the mattress surface; its bottom must not penetrate the bed frame or mattress by more than 0.03 m.
Every site area labeled in the documents (parking, terrace, pool, etc.) must be built in the model with its outline and appropriate ground treatment.
Every room labeled in the documents must be created in the model with its correct label, level, and area.
A wardrobe must have at least 0.50 m of clear space in front of it for its doors to open and be used.
null

Any decorative or furniture piece placed on the top floor must be checked against the underside of the roof (including mansard slopes); if its top exceeds the roof line, it must be lowered, resized, or removed so nothing pokes through the roof.
Ceiling lights must be hung with a visible connection (cord, rod, or canopy) to the ceiling; if no hang record exists, the light must be re-placed with a proper hang fixture or removed.
A scene check that fails on a level after the build stage is a build-stage defect: rerun the build stage so the level's geometry is regenerated and re-checked.

When an armchair faces the back of a sofa and both rotate and swap are refused, the furniture agent's next round must re-place the seating group so the armchair faces the coffee table, not the sofa's back.
A wardrobe that crosses the room outline by a few centimetres must be nudged back inside the wall line by the furniture agent, not left protruding.
A coffee table that overlaps an armchair must be re-placed by the furniture agent so the seating group clears; a move that only trades one overlap for another is refused.
An armchair whose front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the door must be re-placed by the furniture agent to open the circulation path.
A sofa whose front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the door must be re-placed by the furniture agent to open the circulation path.
A floor lamp that stands in front of a window and blocks its light must be moved by the furniture agent to a free spot away from the window.
A stove whose back is not on a wall must be snapped back onto the kitchen run by the furniture agent; a stove floating off the counter line is a misplacement.
A kitchen aisle narrower than 0.90 m in front of the counter must be opened by the furniture agent re-placing the kitchen run or the island to restore the working aisle.
A stove is a wall fixture: its back must sit on the kitchen run's wall, not float 6 cm off it.
A kitchen run must leave at least 0.90 m of aisle in front of it.
A seating group's chairs must face the group's centre; when individual rotations and moves keep failing, re-solve the whole room's AI layout.
A dining chair needs at least 0.81 m from the table edge to the wall or piece behind it.
A sofa's back must rest on a wall; a sofa floating 2 m from any wall is a mis-placed piece.
A sofa's back must rest on a wall.
A seating group's chairs must face the group's centre.
A double bed needs at least 0.60 m of free space along each side.
A nightstand must not stand in front of a window (sill + 0.05 m).
A wardrobe needs at least 0.80 m of free space in front of it.
A shower whose drawn footprint is outside the product range of its assigned model must be swapped to a model whose real size fits the drawn bay, not left at a non-existent size.
When a drawn shower's size is within tolerance of the real range but its assigned model does not match, swap to a model whose real size matches the drawn footprint rather than resizing or rotating.
When a bed's side clearance is below the minimum and moving it individually worsens other findings, re-layout the whole room so the solver can place the bed with adequate clearance on both sides.
When a wardrobe's front clearance is below the minimum and no free wall span exists within the allowed move distance, re-layout the room to find a placement with adequate clearance.
When a bed's side clearance is below the minimum, re-layout the room so the solver can place the bed with adequate clearance.
When a wardrobe's front clearance is below the minimum and moving it does not resolve the finding, re-layout the room.
When a sofa's free zone in front is blocked by another piece, re-layout the room so the solver can arrange the seating group with clear sight and access lines.
When a coffee table is not in front of the sofa, re-layout the room so the seating group is arranged correctly.
When an armchair is too far from the coffee table or at the wrong angle, re-layout the room to fix the seating group geometry.
When a chair's clearance behind is below the minimum, re-layout the room to fix the dining group spacing.
When a sofa's free zone in front is blocked by another piece, re-layout the room.
When a coffee table is not in front of the sofa and individual moves are refused due to drawn-lock constraints, re-layout the room.
When an armchair is too far from the coffee table or at the wrong angle, re-layout the room.
When a dining table stands in front of a window, re-layout the room to move the dining group away from the window.
When a chair stands in front of a window, re-layout the room to move the dining group away from the window.
Inspector findings must name the piece by its recorded type and room, not by a guessed label; a wall_cabinet in a kitchen is a valid upper cabinet and is not a shoe cabinet.
The furniture agent must not drop a placed dining table from a room's set; a dining table is a core member of the dining group and must be re-placed if it is lost between the decor and agent stages.
The furniture agent must not drop a dining chair that belongs to a placed dining table; chairs are members of the dining group and must be re-placed if lost.
The furniture agent must not drop a placed decorative piece (potted plant) from a room; decor pieces placed in the decor stage must be preserved through the agent stage.
The furniture agent must not drop a placed lighting piece (floor lamp) from a room; lighting pieces placed in the decor stage must be preserved through the agent stage.
The furniture agent must not drop a placed seating accessory (ottoman) from a room; seating accessories placed in the decor stage must be preserved through the agent stage.
The furniture agent must not drop a nightstand that belongs to a placed bed; a nightstand is a member of the sleeping group and must be re-placed if lost.
The furniture agent must not drop a placed media unit (tv_unit) from a living room; a tv_unit is a core member of the living set and must be re-placed if lost.
The furniture agent must not drop a placed storage piece (sideboard) from a living room; a sideboard is a member of the living storage set and must be re-placed if lost.
The build stage must place every planned kitchen fixture (stove, sink, counter) in the scene; a planned stove that has no scene object is a build failure and must be re-run.
A planned piece that the build stage leaves without a scene object is a build loss, not a reading error: the build stage must place every planned piece or record why it cannot.
A stair core that fills its room has no free interior camera point; the stair must be shown from the adjoining hall, not from inside the stair.
A piece of the final stage that the build stage drops (named in a conflict) is a build loss: the build stage must keep every final-stage piece or record why it removed it.

When a level is duplicated (two rooms with identical area and identical piece lists), the duplicate is a build-stage artifact; findings on the duplicate that are satisfied by the original room are not real losses.

In a bathroom smaller than 6 m2, if the toilet's side clearance is under 0.38 m and no model swap or rotation can fix it, the finding is a room-size constraint, not a fixable placement error; flag it for architect review rather than looping on model swaps.

In a bathroom smaller than 6 m2, if the bathtub's front clearance is under 0.53 m and the drawn size is within 30% of the real range, the shortfall is a room-size constraint; flag for architect review rather than looping on model swaps.

In a bathroom smaller than 5 m2, if the shower's front clearance is under 0.53 m and the drawn size is within 30% of the real range, the shortfall is a room-size constraint; flag for architect review rather than looping on model swaps.

In a bathroom smaller than 5 m2, if the shower's front clearance is under 0.53 m and both fix_fixture and rotate_piece are refused, the shortfall is a room-size constraint; flag for architect review rather than looping on model swaps.

In a bathroom under a sloped ceiling where the height limit prevents model swaps, if the toilet's side clearance is under 0.38 m, the finding is a room-size and ceiling-height constraint; flag for architect review rather than looping on model swaps.
A drawn bathtub or shower up to 5 cm longer than its bay is a misread size: without center, the code moves it to the nearest valid spot that clears the required front clearance.
A toilet whose centre is under 0.38 m from a side wall or fixture is a placement problem: fix_fixture without center moves it to the nearest valid spot that clears the side clearance.
A washbasin that fails the fit rules under a sloped ceiling (height cap) must take a lower library model that fits the ceiling.
A room typed 'other' that is furnished as a living room (sofa, armchairs, coffee table, dining table) and whose twin is typed 'living' must be retyped to 'living'.

The number of storeys in the model must match the number of storeys shown in the section drawing; if the section shows two storeys, the model must not have more than two levels (excluding basements and terraces).
An opening that is not cut through its wall (the door ray hits the wall) must be fixed by putting the opening back on its wall.

A stair flight must have a handrail over at least 0.72 m of its run; if it does not, the build stage must add a continuous balustrade with newels at its turns and ends, its handrail over the nosing line, stopped under the slab and beside the floor guard of the level above, and a wall handrail where a flight has none.
A frontal view of the entrance (+y) facade must be added if it is missing.
If the terrain slopes up to 1:0.3 (steeper than 1:3), a retaining edge must be built to prevent erosion and ensure stability.
A kitchen counter whose top is over its working height (0.97 m) must take a model that fits the working height.
A dining table on an outdoor terrace must take a lighter, weather-resistant model that is appropriate for outdoor use.
A stair drawn as a slab outline must be built as a full stair (stringers, supports, connection to the floor it lands on); a floating slab with no supports is a build failure, not a drawing feature.
The entrance area must be built as a continuous, connected path (steps, landing, railings) from the ground to the door; floating or disconnected elements are a build failure.
Site areas that are drawn in the plan (pools, terraces) must be registered with their outlines even if the geometry is built separately; 'NOT built (no outline)' for a drawn site area is a loss.
A kitchen counter must be at working height (0.85-0.95 m) with at least 0.90 m aisle in front; a counter at 1.18 m with a 0.55 m aisle is not usable.
The storey count in the model must match the section; a two-storey section must not produce a 3-storey model (L0, L1 plus basement pair).
Room names must be unique per level; two rooms both named 'Yatak Odası 2' on L0 is a reading error that suggests the documents label them as distinct bedrooms.
A drawn piece larger than 4.5 m on a side in a living room is likely a group of drawn pieces that the reading stage failed to split; it must be decomposed into individual furniture items.
A roof terrace drawn in the plan with a door to it must have the roof cut over it; the roof stage must recognize terrace rooms and cut the roof accordingly.

A door whose head would rise above the roof underside at its wall is not a usable door: the roof stage must provide a dormer (or the door is re-read as a window) before the build places it; a door clipped under a sloped roof is a defect, not a placement.
A stage that ends 'pending' with written questions must be answered in the next agent round before the run is considered complete; pending questions are a defect, not a normal stop.
A sofa's front is its long side; a front read on the short side is a recognition error and must be corrected to the long side facing the most open room.
A bench's front is its long side; a front read on the short side is a recognition error and must be corrected to the long side, with its back on the wall.
A scene check failure on a built decor item must be resolved in the next agent round by inspecting the scene check output and correcting the item; a failed scene check is a defect, not a normal stop.
The big loop must run at least one cycle and raise the house score before the run is considered complete; 0 cycles with no score improvement is a defect.
Views marked for review must be inspected and corrected in the next agent round; a view left in review is a defect, not a normal stop.
The build stage must record a leaf state (open or closed) for every inside door; an inside door stands open by default (UL116), and a door with no recorded leaf state is a defect.
The build stage must open a door when a camera view looks through it into a room worth showing (UL126); a view that shows only a closed door where an open door would reveal a room is a defect.

When a tv_unit (or similar long low piece) cannot be placed on any wall span because doors and windows block all free stretches, the agent must either (a) swap to a shorter model that fits a free span, or (b) the room's wall layout must be re-read; a tv_unit that cannot rest on a wall is a defect that requires a model swap or a geometry correction, not repeated move attempts.

When a nightstand stands in front of a window and cannot be moved (overlaps the bed) or swapped (style/fit mismatch), the window's sill must be raised (raise_sill to 0.90 m) or the nightstand must be removed; a nightstand blocking a window is a defect that requires a window adjustment or piece removal, not repeated move/swap attempts.

A seating group (sofa, armchairs, lounge chairs) must be chosen from one style family and a coherent palette; the furniture agent must verify the set before placing, and a single clashing piece is a defect of the whole group.
Every visible horizontal surface in a furnished room (coffee table, TV unit, sideboard) must carry styled decor objects; a bare surface is a defect.
A client-facing render must show a coherent, styled room (matching furniture set, rug, layered lighting, styled surfaces); a flat 'grey box' render is a defect.
A large seating group must sit on a rug that anchors the room; a bare floor under the main seating is a defect.
Full-height window walls in a living room must have layered curtains (sheer and drape); bare glass is a defect.
Every visible horizontal surface in a furnished room must carry styled decor objects; a bare surface is a defect.
A seating group (sofa, armchairs, dining chairs) must be chosen from one style family and a coherent palette; a single clashing piece is a defect of the whole group.
A client-facing render must show a coherent, styled room (matching furniture set, styled surfaces, proper lighting); a flat 'grey box' render is a defect.
Dining chairs at one table must be a matching set in style and colour; a single clashing chair is a defect.
A dining table in a furnished room must carry a table setting (plates, glasses, centerpiece); a bare table is a defect.
A bathroom render must show the main fixtures (bathtub, toilet, washbasin) and styled surfaces with warm lighting; a render that omits the bathtub is a defect.
A bathroom must have warm, layered lighting that creates an inviting glow and contrast; flat grey lighting is a defect.
A bathroom camera must frame the room as a whole, showing the main fixtures; a close-up of a corner or a single small object is a defect.
A bathroom camera must frame the room as a whole, showing the main fixtures; a tight close-up that omits the main fixtures is a defect.
A bathroom camera must frame the room as a whole, showing the main fixtures; a camera positioned too close and at an awkward angle is a defect.
A bathroom camera must frame the room's layout and main fixtures; a close-up that fails to show the layout is a defect.
An interior camera must be posed to show the room's doors, windows and openings, not pressed against a bare wall corner.
A hall or living room render must include a rug or floor treatment to define the space; a bare flat floor is not client-ready.
Furniture in a living room must be a coherent, styled set matching the project's modern aesthetic; blocky low-poly placeholders and mismatched traditional pieces are not acceptable.
A sofa model must match the room's modern/minimal aesthetic; blocky low-poly placeholders with crude piping are not acceptable.
A dining table must match the room's modern/minimal aesthetic; a dark traditional table with turned legs is a mismatch.
A sofa model must match the room's modern/minimal aesthetic; bare boxy models without styling are not acceptable.
A living room render must include a rug to anchor the seating area; a bare flat floor is not client-ready.
A living room render must include styling layers (rug, art, soft furnishings) to be client-ready; a grey-box placeholder is not acceptable.
A large empty wall behind a sofa in a living room must have art, panels, or texture; a completely bare wall is a significant omission.
Furniture in a living room must be a coherent, styled set; mismatched blocky models are not client-ready.
The exterior environment in a render must have realistic ground texture, varied vegetation, and a proper sky; a flat untextured green field with low-poly lollipop trees is not client-ready.
The view through a window must show a realistic landscape with depth, vegetation, and ground detail; a flat untextured green plane is not acceptable.
A potted plant model must look realistic with variation and texture; crude low-poly clumps of blades are not acceptable.
A balcony dining table should have a table setting to look lived-in; a bare table is not client-ready.
Balcony chairs must match the table's style; white plastic garden chairs with an industrial metal table look accidental and cheap.
The exterior environment in a render must have realistic ground texture, varied vegetation, and a proper sky; a broken grey-box environment undermines the render.
Outdoor terrace furniture must be a coherent set (matching material family) and the ground must carry a real grass texture, not a flat green plane.
The site ground must be given a real grass (or paving) look, never a flat untextured green plane.
Exterior presentation renders must show finished facade materials, landscaping and warm lighting, not a grey-box massing.
Exterior night/evening renders must include warm interior lighting so rooms glow through the glazing.
Exterior renders must show a structurally supported staircase and finished materials, not a floating stair in a void.
An exterior view must be framed at eye level (1.5-1.7 m) or above the ridge, never pressed against a wall from above the roofline.
Exterior presentation renders must show finished materials, landscaping and depth, not a sterile grey-box void.
Exterior presentation renders must show the specified cladding, landscaping and architectural detailing, not a raw massing study.

Every drawn furniture symbol must be typed by a rule or model; if a symbol cannot be matched to a known type, the reading stage must flag it for manual typing rather than leaving it 'unknown' and unbuilt.
Decor that cannot find a valid resting surface on its host is correctly left unbuilt rather than floating.
Decor that penetrates its host beyond tolerance is correctly left unbuilt rather than showing the host through the cloth.
Decor that cannot rest within tolerance of its host is correctly left unbuilt rather than floating.

A small decor item (plant, book, throw) assigned to a host whose built top is not a single flat surface (no top found, or the top tears) must be dropped from the scene rather than left as a failed, un-built rest; the decor stage should verify the host exposes a flat top before placing it.
A soft decor (throw) must not be placed on a host whose top is not one continuous surface (tears > 0.25 m) or that pokes through the cloth; the decor stage should drop it.
A decor item whose rest gap to its host exceeds 0.01 m must be dropped rather than left un-built.
A small decor item assigned to a host with no built top must be dropped from the scene.
Every camera dropped by the camera stage must carry a recorded reason (e.g. blocked, duplicate, bare wall); a drop with no reason is a defect and the view must be restored.
A drawn block whose name and size match a known fixture (e.g. a small cabinet or appliance) must be mapped to a piece in the model; an unmapped named block is a reading loss.
A drawn block named 'merdiven' (stair) must be mapped to a stair piece in the model; an unmapped stair block is a reading loss.
A drawn block whose name is not a known furniture or fixture symbol and whose size does not match any buildable piece is recorded as a drawing mark, not a lost element.
A drawn block that is site decor (landscaping, paving, pool furniture) is recorded as a site symbol, not a lost interior element.
A drawn stair symbol that is already represented by a built stair piece in the model is not a lost element.
Blocks under 0.10 m on one side that sit on dimension or annotation layers are marks, not furniture or structure, and are not built.
Sheet-frame and title-block blocks are drawing furniture, not building elements, and are never built into the model.
Small square symbol blocks that are tags or markers rather than furniture footprints are not built; only blocks whose size and context match a furniture or fixture type are modelled.
Entities on layers that are off or frozen in the source DWG are not read, because the author has hidden them from the active design.
OLE2FRAME and WIPEOUT entities are non-geometric (embedded objects and masks) and are never read as building elements.
Structural columns that stand out of the wall band are not modelled as walls; they are separate structural elements outside the wall-building scope.
A drawn symbol that both reading passes classify as not_furniture is kept as an obstacle and not built, unless an architect action reclassifies it.
Elements drawn on structural layers (e.g. 'A-BA') are treated as structure, not furniture, and are not built as furniture pieces.

A small drawn piece (tap, drain, handle) that sits 60% or more inside a larger fixture of the same set is a part of that fixture, not a duplicate; the reading merges it and the ledger must not flag the merge as a lost piece.

When two pieces of the same type overlap and one is drawn inside the other, the larger is the piece and the smaller is its inner symbol (shade, base); the reading keeps the larger and the ledger must not flag the inner symbol as a lost piece.
Layers whose name indicates 2D annotation (axis bubbles, dimensions, text) are not part of the 3D model; the ledger must not flag their entities as lost.
Layers whose name indicates decoration or finish (tile patterns, floor texture) are not part of the 3D model; the ledger must not flag their entities as lost.
Layers whose name indicates finish or annotation (vitrification, coating) are not part of the 3D model; the ledger must not flag their entities as lost.
The agent must not remove a piece that is the defining fixture of a room's program (e.g. a shoe cabinet in a hall) unless the room's program explicitly excludes it.
When the build stage drops a piece as part of a conflict cluster, the ledger must flag it as lost and the build stage must be re-run to restore it.
A bench is not a type allowed in an 'other' room; the reading must retype it to a type that fits the room (e.g. console_table) or the room type must be changed.

When a room outline holds the labels of two rooms (e.g. 'Salon' and 'AÇIK MUTFAK'), the reading must check for a missing wall between them and split the room into two if the labels indicate different room types.

A drawn piece that is off its drawn centre by more than the 0.05 m tolerance must be moved back to its drawn position (or the nearest free spot within the 0.3 m drawn-lock) before the render check, so the layout stage, not the render stage, owns drawn-piece placement.

An interior bathroom camera must frame the whole wet set (bathtub, washbasin, toilet, tall cabinet) so the render shows a complete, furnished bathroom, not a bare wall with a partially visible fixture.

A site area drawn on the plan (parking, terrace, pool) must be built as a site element (outline, paving, or pool) in the site stage; if the drawing shows it, the site stage must not leave it as 'NOT built (no outline)'.

A zone label that names a kitchen (e.g. 'AÇIK MUTFAK') inside a room typed living must split the room into a living part and a kitchen part (or retype the room kitchen) so the kitchen is checked and furnished as its own space, not absorbed into the living room.
A ceiling light placed under a sloped ceiling must be hung flush with the slope (its top at the local ceiling height), not at a fixed height that leaves a gap under the slope.

When the fitting stage falls back to a parametric mesh for a piece, the next round must swap it to a library model that matches the project's style chain and passes the fit rules, rather than leaving the parametric placeholder.

When a wall_cabinet run is built, its unit joints must be aligned to the base units' joints directly beneath it; the kitchen module builder must snap the upper run's divisions to the lower run's divisions so no joint is left unpaired.
A bedroom is not required to have a TV; the room is correctly furnished as a bedroom (bed, nightstand, wardrobe) and the code already refused every TV placement because the view is blocked.
A bathroom's program includes storage; when the bathroom set is built without a storage unit, the layout stage must add the missing storage group so the fixtures are not left standing alone.
A living room must be furnished to at least 25% of its floor; when the layout stage leaves wide empty floor, it must re-place the pieces (relayout) to fill the room to the furnished threshold.

A bathroom's program includes a storage element (tall_cabinet or wall_cabinet); the room_fill stage must place one whenever the room has no storage piece, so its fixtures are never left standing alone.

A bedroom's accent wall must carry a feature finish (fluted/panelled) and the wood floor a parquet look; the decor stage's professional dressing and the build's finishes must apply both so the room meets the professional bar.

A bed's bedding set must include a deep duvet whose hem overhangs the free foot side (about 0.24 m) and a woven, fringed throw pair; the decor bedding plan and the build's textiles.bedding_set must apply both.
A bed's bedding set must include a woven, fringed throw pair laid across the foot; the decor bedding plan and the build's textiles.bedding_set must place it.
A kitchen worktop must carry a few small props (a fruit bowl, a kettle, a cutting board) so the counter reads as inhabited and designed, not empty.
Interior door frames must match the room's palette; in a light, modern hallway the door and its frame take a light painted finish, not a dark heavy one.
An office chair must match the room's style and palette; a generic black dated model is not acceptable in a light-wood modern room, so the fit stage must pick a modern model from the allowed list.
A wardrobe must be built from a textured, finished library model, not a flat untextured slab; the build stage must assign a real wardrobe model with visible material.
A living room's main wall behind the sofa must carry wall art and decor to anchor the space; the decor stage must place it, not leave the wall bare.
A console table and a coffee table must carry styled surfaces (books, a vase, a decorative tray) so they read as lived-in, not as an empty showroom.
A balcony's program includes a place to sit (a chair or a small table with seating); the layout stage must place a balcony group so the outdoor space reads as livable, not a construction site.

Facade window/door joinery must vary in material and size to create rhythm; a monotonous plain repetitive joinery is not acceptable, so the build stage must mix materials (wood, stone, glass) and vary sizes.
A window that reads as a dark slatted grille louver is a placeholder and clashes with clean modern glazing; the build stage must assign a clean modern glazing look, not a louver.
A dining table must carry a table setting (plates, a bowl or a vase) so it reads as set for use, not empty.
A desk with a facing seat must carry a work set (a laptop or computer on it facing the seat) so the seat reads as used, not facing nothing.
When a decor element's host piece is not built, the build stage must either build the host or explicitly record why the host is excluded; silently dropping the host and all its children is a loss.
A drawn symbol that both recognition passes classify as not_furniture is kept as an obstacle and is not built as a piece; this is correct behaviour, not a loss.
A drawn outline that encloses a table and its chairs and is mostly empty space is a rug mark, not a furniture piece; it is handled by the decor stage, not built as a piece.
Cushions that belong to a piece's family cushion set are built as part of that piece's dressing, not as separate pieces; this is correct behaviour.
Cushions and pillows that are part of a library model are not separate pieces; they are included in the model and not built individually.
When two floor lamps of the same room are drawn overlapping (one inside the other), they are one lamp drawn twice; the larger one is kept and the smaller duplicate is not built.
A small ottoman drawn mostly inside an armchair is the armchair's seat cushion, not a separate piece; it is not built.

When a plan carries a zone label for a kitchen (e.g. 'AÇIK MUTFAK') inside a room that also holds living furniture, the room is an open-plan living/kitchen space: the reading stage must record the kitchen zone as a sub-zone of the room (keeping the room type living) and the build stage must place the kitchen run within that zone, so the kitchen is not lost or mis-typed.
A piece typed by context from its size and neighbours is correct when it fits its room and the drawing; the absence of a codified rule for the inference is not a defect in the built model.
When a table/desk symbol's drawn footprint includes its chair, the desk is sized to the table portion and the chair is placed as a separate piece in front; this is correct handling, not a misread.
Kitchen fixtures in a living room are valid when the layout is an open-plan kitchen; the room type remains living and the kitchen zone is a sub-zone.
A sofa's front must face the open floor and its partner; when the front is inferred, it should be set explicitly to the direction that looks into the most open floor.
An armchair's front must face away from its wall or towards its partner; when the front is inferred, it should be set explicitly.
A living room without a TV unit does not require a TV wall; the absence of a suitable wall for a TV is not a defect when no TV is present.
A bedroom without a TV unit does not require a TV wall; the absence of a suitable wall for a TV is not a defect when no TV is present.
A media-wall / TV placement check must be skipped for rooms whose program does not include a TV (bedrooms, bathrooms, halls); a missing TV in a non-living room is not a defect.
When a plan labels a room as a terrace/balcony with a door to it, the roof stage must cut an opening in the roof over that room (a roof terrace), not build the roof closed over it.
When a door on the top floor would reach above the roof underside at its wall, the roof stage must provide a dormer or cut the roof to give the door full headroom (at least 2.0 m clear).
Ceiling lights without a host room are generic decor; a size cap warning on them is informational and does not require action.
When a door's top is above the roof underside at its wall, the door height must be clipped to the roof underside minus a clearance, or the roof must be raised/cut to accommodate the door.
Ceiling lights under sloped ceilings should be hung flush under the slope; a warning about this is informational and does not require action.

A cushion placed on a bed must rest on the mattress surface; its bottom face may not penetrate the mattress by more than 0.03 m. The decor stage must verify the resting height of every soft item against the support it sits on and nudge it up to the surface if it intersects.
Every site area the documents label (parking, terrace, pool, etc.) must be built as an outdoor space with its outline; the site stage must not drop a labelled area without a recorded reason.

Every room label the documents place on a level must be matched to a model room on that level; the reading stage must not leave a labelled room unassigned when a model room of the same size and position exists.

When a bathroom is under a sloped ceiling, the fit rules must allow the standard bathroom fixtures (washbasin, toilet, bathtub) to be placed at their working heights even if the ceiling at that point is below the generic 1.60 m cap, provided the fixture's own height is below the local ceiling; the sloped-ceiling cap must be applied per-fixture-height, not as a blanket 1.60 m limit that rejects every washbasin model.

A wardrobe (or any front-opening storage) is placed only on a wall span that leaves at least its door-swing depth (0.50 m) clear in front; if no such span exists in the room, the piece is not placed rather than parked against a blocked wall.

Any decorative or furniture piece whose top exceeds the clear ceiling height of its room (ceiling minus the piece's own clearance) is rejected at placement and re-seated lower or removed; a piece is never allowed to poke through the roof or ceiling.

Every stair with an open side (no wall or balustrade along its full run) is built with a safety railing/guard on that open side as part of the stair assembly; a stair is never placed without a guard on its open edge.
Every stair opening (void) in a floor is built with a safety railing/guard around its open edges as part of the floor build; a stair opening is never left unguarded.

A camera view that renders entirely black or empty (no room, no main group, no architecture at eye height) is a failed render and must be re-run through the layout/room_fill stage before it is accepted.

A wardrobe (or any storage run) is built from a library model that renders as a functional storage unit with doors or handles, not as a flat wall panel; if the only available model for the run's length renders as a panel, the run is split into shorter modules or a different model is used.

Scene check S5 (detached elements) must pass for every level before the build stage is accepted; any element that fails S5 is re-seated or removed in the build stage, not carried forward to the final stage.
Every ceiling light is built with a hang record (cord, rod, or canopy) connecting it to the ceiling; a ceiling light is never placed without a visible or recorded connection to the ceiling above it.
Scene check S1 (geometry) must pass for every level before the build stage is accepted; any element that fails S1 is re-seated or removed in the build stage, not carried forward to the final stage.
Scene check S2 (geometry) must pass for every level before the build stage is accepted; any element that fails S2 is re-seated or removed in the build stage, not carried forward to the final stage.
A scene check that fails on a level is a build-stage defect: re-run the build stage for that level so the geometry is regenerated and re-checked.

When an armchair faces the back of another seat and rotation is refused because it would face a wall, the furniture agent's next round must re-place the seating group so each seat faces the shared table, not a neighbour's back.
A piece that crosses a room outline by 0.02 m or less is within tolerance and is not a defect.

When a coffee table overlaps a seat and every move is refused (it would still overlap or break a clearance), the furniture agent's next round must re-solve the seating group so the table clears every seat.
When a seat's front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the room door, the furniture agent's next round must re-place the seating so the approach to each seat is clear.
When a sofa's front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway from the room door, the furniture agent's next round must re-place the seating so the approach to the sofa is clear.
A floor lamp must not stand in front of a window: the furniture agent's next round must place it clear of the window's sight and light line.

When a coffee table overlaps a seat and every move is refused (it would still overlap, break a clearance, or exceed the move limit), the furniture agent's next round must re-solve the seating group so the table clears every seat.
A stove or any back-to-wall kitchen fixture must be placed flush against a wall; a gap greater than 0.03 m is a placement error, not a tolerance.
A kitchen counter run must leave at least 0.90 m of clear aisle in front of it; a tighter aisle is a placement error.
When individual rotate/move edits of a seating group keep failing the facing and clearance checks, re-solve the whole room's AI layout so the group is placed coherently.
A dining chair needs at least 0.81 m from the table edge to the wall or piece behind it; a tighter gap is a placement error.
A sofa's back must rest on a wall; a sofa floating 2 m from any wall is a missing-wall placement error.
A sofa's back must rest on a wall; a gap greater than 0.03 m is a placement error.
A double bed needs at least 0.60 m of free space along each side; a tighter gap is a placement error.
A nightstand must not stand in front of a window; it must be placed clear of the window's sill and swing.
A wardrobe needs at least 0.80 m of free space in front of it for the doors to open; a tighter gap is a placement error.
A piece that blocks a window's clear zone (sill + 0.05 m) is moved to the nearest free place in its room, clear of the opening.
A wardrobe with less than 0.80 m in front is moved to a free place that gives its full opening clearance.
A drawn shower whose size is outside the product range is corrected to a real product size that fits its bay.
A bed with less than 0.60 m along its side is moved to a free place that gives its full side clearance.
A piece that blocks the free zone in front of a sofa is moved to a free place that clears the sofa's front.
A coffee table not in front of the sofa is moved to the free place in front of it.
An armchair that is too far from the coffee table is moved to a free place within 2.50 m of it.
A chair with less than 0.81 m behind it is moved to a free place that gives its full clearance.
A chair or any piece whose seat height exceeds a window sill plus 0.05 m must not be placed in front of that window; the furniture agent must keep a clear zone in front of every window.
A shoe cabinet must be built from a dedicated shoe-cabinet model, never from a generic wall_cabinet/wall_run module; the build stage must match the piece type to a model of the same type.

The furniture agent must not drop decor-stage pieces (dining table, chairs, plants, lamps, ottoman, tv_unit, sideboard) when re-placing a room; every decor-stage piece must be carried into the agent stage.
The furniture agent must not drop decor-stage pieces when re-placing a room; every decor-stage piece must be carried into the agent stage.

A planned piece whose model is a module of another piece (a stove or sink inside the kitchen run) must be built as its own object; the build stage must not drop a planned piece because its model is shared with a neighbour.
A stair core room whose only camera point is inside the stair must be shown from the adjacent hall; the camera stage must place the view in the hall looking at the stair, not inside the stair volume.
A piece named in a conflict resolution must survive the build stage; the build stage must not drop a piece that the conflict resolver kept.

A drawn piece in a kitchen that is not a recognised kitchen fixture and whose retype to a plausible type is refused on overlap must be kept as a parametric piece and built, not left untyped and unbuilt with no warning.
When a level's rooms are dropped by the build stage as a conflict cluster, its drawn furniture is not a separate reading loss; restore the level first.
Kitchen fixtures in a room dropped by the build stage are not separate reading losses; restore the room first.

Stair layers (A-MERDIVEN, A-merdiven görünüş) must be read and a stair piece placed on every level that has a stair, even when the level's rooms are in a build conflict cluster; the stair is structural and must not be dropped with the rooms.
Stair elevation layers (A-merdiven görünüş) must be read to inform the stair piece placement on every level that has a stair, even when the level's rooms are in a build conflict cluster.
Decorative layers (Deko_*, Vitrifiye) are drawing decorations and are not expected to be used by the model; they should not be flagged as lost.
Vitrification/finish layers (Piu_Vitrifiye, *_Vitrifiye) are drawing finish layers and are not expected to be used by the model; they should not be flagged as lost.

The build stage must not drop an entire room because a single kitchen fixture (e.g. fridge) is missing from the kitchen zone; it should build the room and flag the missing fixture for the furniture agent to add.
The build stage must not drop an entire level's rooms because of a single kitchen fixture issue in one room; each room should be evaluated independently.
The build stage must not drop kitchen fixtures because a single fixture (e.g. fridge) is missing; it should build the kitchen zone with the available fixtures and flag the missing one.
Stoves and other wall-mounted kitchen fixtures should be snapped to their wall; a gap of 0.06 m is a drawing artifact, not a real gap.
A wall-adjacent fixture read from the plan must be snapped flush to its wall; a residual gap of more than 0.02 m between the fixture back and the wall is a reading error, not a clearance.
A kitchen room's program requires a fridge; when the drawn kitchen run lacks one, the run is re-solved as a unit to add the missing member rather than leaving the room incomplete.

When a toilet's side clearance is short by less than 0.05 m and no model swap or rotation can fix it, the fixture is re-centred within its bay to maximise the minimum side clearance; if the bay itself is too narrow, the room's layout is flagged for the architect rather than forcing a non-compliant fit.

A bathtub's front clearance is governed by the room's layout, not the model; when the drawn bay leaves less than 0.53 m in front, the room's fixture arrangement is re-solved (or the architect is asked to confirm the tight fit) rather than swapping to a shorter tub that still does not clear.

A shower's front clearance is governed by the room's layout; when the drawn bay leaves less than 0.53 m in front, the room's fixture arrangement is re-solved or the architect confirms the tight fit, rather than swapping to a model that still does not clear.
A drawn bathtub/shower is placed at its drawn centre; when the resulting front clearance is under the minimum, the code must re-seat it to the nearest valid spot (not just flag it).
A toilet whose centre is under 0.38 m from a side wall/fixture must be re-seated to the nearest valid spot, not just flagged.
An entry hall must carry an entrance group (bench/console/mirror) to anchor the entry; the furniture agent must place it when the hall is otherwise bare.
A room's type must match its fixtures and furniture; a 40.5 m2 room furnished as a living room (sofa, armchairs, coffee table, dining table) is 'living', not 'other'.
A circulation room that holds a stair plus a wardrobe/shoe cabinet is a 'hall' (a hall with a stair), not a 'stair' room; the type 'hall' is correct.

The storey count must be read from the section/elevation, not inferred from the number of floor levels in the plan; a two-storey building with a basement and a mezzanine is still two storeys above ground.
An opening must be cut through its wall; if the door ray hits a wall, the opening is not cut and must be re-cut.
A stair flight must have a handrail over its full run; if a flight has no handrail over 0.72 m of its run, the build stage must add a wall handrail or a balustrade.
Every facade must have a frontal exterior camera view; if the +y facade has none, the camera stage must add one.
When the terrain slopes steeper than 1:3, a retaining edge (retaining wall or stepped plinth) must be built at the building's perimeter.
A kitchen counter's top must be at its working height (0.90-0.97 m); if the model's top is higher, the build stage must use a model at the correct height.

A kitchen counter (kitchen_run) must be built with its worktop at the standard working height (0.90-0.95 m); a counter whose top is placed above 1.00 m is a misread and must be corrected to working height before the run is accepted.
Every interior room must be lit in the render (ceiling or wall light, or daylight through its windows); a room rendered with no visible light source is a failed render and must be re-lit.
The outdoor environment (lawn, trees, ground) must be a believable landscape, not a flat untextured plane with low-poly placeholder trees; a placeholder site is a failed render.
Entrance steps and railings must clearly connect to a path and a door; floating railings or steps that do not link to a circulation path are a build error.

Site areas that are drawn and labelled in the documents (pools, terraces, parking) must be registered with their outlines in the model; a site area recorded 'NOT built (no outline)' when the documents show it is a loss.

A kitchen must have a worktop at working height (0.90-0.95 m) and a clear aisle of at least 0.90 m in front of it; a kitchen with a counter above working height and an aisle under 0.90 m is not usable and must be corrected.

The storey count of the model must match the section drawing; if the section shows two storeys, the model must not have three (or vice versa). A basement pair (L-1/L-1b) that the section does not show is a misread.
Room names must be unique per level; if the documents label two distinct bedrooms, the model must not give them the same name. Duplicate room names on the same level are a reading error.

A drawn piece larger than 4.5 m on a side in a living room is a group of pieces, not a single furniture item; it must be split into its constituent pieces and typed individually, not left as an untyped cluster.
A room-type finding must be re-checked against the model's current type before being raised: if the model already carries the correct type, the finding is a false alarm and is closed, not re-fixed.

When the plan draws a roof terrace (a room labelled terrace on the top level, with a door to it), the roof stage must cut the roof over that room's footprint and add a guard on its open edges, instead of closing the roof over it.

When a top-floor door or window head would be clipped by a sloped roof underside, the roof stage must provide a dormer (or a flat roof pocket) over that opening so the full door/window height is usable.
A stage that ends 'pending' with open questions must be rerun (or the questions answered) before the run is considered complete; a pending stage is a failed step, not a finished one.

A sofa (or any long piece) read with its front on a short side is a reading error: the front must be set on the long side facing the most open space, and the build step must be rerun when this is detected.

A console table (or any long, narrow piece) read with its front on a short side is a reading error: the front must be set on the long side with the back on the wall, and the build step must be rerun when this is detected.
A scene check failure (S5) for a built decor item must trigger a rerun of the build/scene step for that level so the item is corrected before the run is considered complete.
Views marked for review must be re-evaluated (rerun the render/check stage) before the run is considered complete; a view left in 'review' is an open item.
Inside doors must stand open by default in the build (door_states); a door with no leaf state recorded is a build error and the door_states step must be rerun.
A door that a camera view sees into a room worth showing must stand open in that view (door_states.revise_for_cameras); a closed door in such a view is a build error.

A wardrobe whose drawn footprint is deeper than the clearance its room allows must be swapped to a shallower model of the same type (depth <= 0.55 m) rather than moved, so its front clearance meets the minimum without leaving its wall.
A toilet that sits above its floor (a raised or wall-hung model) must be swapped to a floor-standing model whose base rests on the floor, not moved.
A washbasin whose lowest point is above its floor (a wall-hung or raised model) must be swapped to a floor-standing or counter model that rests on the floor, not moved.
A coffee table that overlaps a seating piece and cannot be moved within the drawn-lock limit must be swapped to a smaller model that fits the free zone, not moved.

A drawn piece longer than 4.5 m and no deeper than 0.70 m in a living or dining room is a built-in storage run; the reader must split it into a run of standard-depth (0.40-0.60 m) cabinets rather than leaving it untyped.
A wardrobe that reaches up to 0.020 m through the room outline is within tolerance and must not be flagged as F9.
An armchair whose front use zone is not reached by a 0.60 m walkway from a door is acceptable when the armchair is part of a seating group that is itself reachable.
A floor lamp standing in front of a window is acceptable when the lamp is shorter than the window head and does not block the view.
A kitchen that has a fridge in its drawn set is not missing a fridge, even if the fridge is in a different room.
A toilet whose centre is 0.33 m from the side wall is acceptable when the toilet is 0.50 m wide (the gap on the other side is >= 0.38 m).
A sofa whose free zone in front is blocked by a coffee table is acceptable when the coffee table is part of the seating group.
A toilet model that is a crude, low-poly box must be swapped to a realistic toilet model with a proper cistern shape.

A living room's seating group (sofa, armchairs, coffee table) must be a coherent set: same style family and a limited palette (max 2 accent colours), with a rug under the group and styled surfaces (books, vases, throws) on the coffee table and TV unit.
A dining set (table + chairs) must be a coherent group: same style family and material, with a table setting (plates, glasses) on the table.
A bathroom of 5 m2 or more must include a bathtub as its anchor fixture, with warm lighting and styled surfaces (towels, plants, decor) to match the reference standard.
An interior camera must frame the room's main fixtures from a free point with headroom, not a close-up of a corner.
A bedroom render must show layered bedding, styled surfaces and a feature wall to meet the project's presentation standard.
A bedroom's surfaces (nightstand, console) must carry styled objects (mirror, vase, books) to look finished.
A bed must show layered bedding (throw, second blanket, euro shams) to meet the presentation standard.
A bedroom render must show soft furnishings, lighting, and architectural details to meet the project's standard.
An interior camera must frame the room's floor and main furniture, not a corner and a door leaf at a low angle.
An office chair in a residential bedroom must be a softer, upholstered or wood chair that matches the bed and desk, not a corporate black leather piece.
A desk in a modern, minimalist bedroom must be a modern, minimalist piece, not a dated, traditional Shaker-style piece.
A bedroom's wall behind the bed must be a feature wall (e.g., vertical fluted or slatted wood panelling) to anchor the bed.
A bedroom render must show a rug, layered curtains, warm light, styled surfaces, and layered bedding to meet the project's standard.
A wardrobe in a modern, minimalist bedroom must have a refined finish that matches the headboard and walls, not a raw, light wood that looks unfinished.
A bedroom render must show a feature wall, rug, curtains, layered bedding, and a styled desk to meet the project's standard.
A bed must show layered bedding (throw, second blanket, euro shams) and its base must match the room's palette.
A desk must carry a work set (laptop, books, decor) to look believable.
An interior camera must frame the room's main fixtures from a free point with headroom, not a black, empty frame.
A hall or corridor render must include at least one styling layer (rug, art, or lighting) and the camera must not frame a bare wall; a grey-box corridor is not client-ready.
Every hall or corridor must carry a floor styling layer (rug or runner) in the furnished model so renders are not bare.
A corridor camera must look down the corridor axis and show its doors, not the side of a storage piece; a side-on wardrobe view is a bad pose.
A living/activity room render must use coherent, textured furniture in one style and include styling layers (rug, throws, art); blocky grey-box placeholders are not client-ready.
A sofa must use a real product model (not a generated placeholder with guessed units) when a real product of the type fits within the caps.
A dining table in a modern/minimal room must use a model matching the room's style; a dark traditional table with turned legs is a mismatch.
A living/activity room must have a rug under the seating group to anchor the space; a bare untextured floor is not client-ready.
A living/activity room render must use coherent, textured furniture in one style and include styling layers; blocky grey-box placeholders are not client-ready.
A large empty wall behind a sofa or console must carry art, a feature panel, or texture; a completely bare wall is a significant omission for a client-ready image.
An exterior or terrace render must show a textured, detailed environment (lawn, varied trees, hedges); a flat untextured green plane and identical low-poly trees are not client-ready.
A terrace or balcony floor must use a designed outdoor material (paving, decking, stone); a bare untextured grey slab is not client-ready.
An exterior or terrace render must show a textured, detailed environment; a flat untextured green plane is not client-ready.
An exterior or terrace render must show a textured, detailed environment; a flat untextured lawn and identical low-poly trees are not client-ready.
A terrace dining table must have a table setting (cloth, place settings) to read as a designed outdoor dining surface; a bare table on a bare slab is not client-ready.
A balcony or terrace render must show a coherent, finished outdoor furniture set on a finished floor (decking or paving) with planters; a mismatched set on a bare slab is not client-ready.
Exterior renders must be lit by a warm sun (not flat grey) and show a finished facade plus a landscaped site (paths, planters, trees); a grey-box massing study is not client-ready.
Exterior and facade views must carry a warm sun and warm interior light glowing through the windows; a flat overcast grey render is not client-ready.
Exterior renders must show a finished facade (cladding/texture) and landscape integration (mature planting, defined paths); a sterile massing study is not client-ready.
A balcony or veranda must carry a place to sit (a balcony group: seating plus a table); a bare slab with no lounging area is not a finished outdoor space.
Exterior views must carry architectural/garden lighting (warm sun, a defined path, planters) so the facade and approach read as inviting; a completely unlit exterior is not client-ready.
An exterior view must frame the whole building from a valid eye-level or aerial position; a close-up that cuts off the building and focuses on a corner is not a valid presentation view.
Exterior renders must show a finished, styled home (crisp cladding, defined entrance, landscaped garden with places to sit); a grey-box massing study is not client-ready.
Exterior renders must show material richness (cladding, stone), landscaping and architectural detailing (canopies, railings); a raw grey-box massing study in a void is not client-ready.

Every drawn furniture symbol must be typed by a rule or model, or explicitly marked as a non-furniture symbol with its recognition crop; a drawn piece left 'unknown' with nothing built and nothing explaining it is a reading loss.
Decor that rests on a host must find a valid top on the built host; if the host has no restable top, the decor is dropped rather than left floating or unplaced.
A throw or cloth decor must rest on its host with penetration within tolerance (<= 0.007 m); if the host shows through the cloth, the decor is re-seated or dropped.
A throw or cloth decor must rest on its host with penetration within tolerance (<= 0.007 m); if the host pokes through the cloth, the decor is re-seated or dropped.
A bowl or small decor must rest on its host with a gap within tolerance (<= 0.01 m); if the gap is larger, the decor is re-seated or dropped.
not_a_problem

The reading stage must read entities on off or frozen layers (or explicitly log every skipped layer with its entity count) so the ledger can verify that no load-bearing geometry was hidden; silently skipping invisible layers is not allowed.
guards.target: # entities on layers that are off or frozen (or invisible) were not read

guards.rule: The camera stage must record a reason whenever it drops a view (or keep the view); a camera may never be removed silently.

The reading stage must map every drawn block/insert on a plan to a model element (a piece, a fixture, or an explicit 'not furniture' mark); a drawn block that no element uses is a loss and must be accounted for.
A drawn block whose name is not a known furniture or fixture symbol and whose size does not match any library piece is a drawing mark, not a piece: the reading stage records it and does not build it.
A drawn block that is a site-decor symbol (landscaping, paving, pool furniture) is recorded as site decor and not built as a house piece.
A drawn stair block is read as the stair piece of the room it sits in; when the room already has a built stair, the block is the same stair and is not a lost piece.

Two floor-lamp outlines of the same room where the smaller is drawn inside the larger are one lamp drawn with two outlines; the reading keeps the larger and the ledger must not flag the smaller as a lost piece.

A DWG layer whose name is a generic 2D/annotation tag (2D, TEXT, DIM, AXIS) holding only circles and lines is reference geometry, not furniture or structure; the model may ignore it without a warning.

A DWG layer whose name denotes a decorative finish pattern (Deko, Zemin, Seramik, tile, pattern) holding arcs/ellipses/splines is a 2D finish hatch, not furniture or structure; the model may ignore it without a warning.

A DWG layer whose name denotes a decorative finish (VITR, vitrification, glaze) holding only arcs and lines is a 2D finish hatch, not furniture or structure; the model may ignore it without a warning.
The furniture agent must not remove a drawn piece that is the defining storage of a hall/entrance (shoe cabinet); if it does not fit, it is re-typed or moved, never deleted.

When the build stage drops a drawn piece as part of a level conflict cluster, the conflict must be resolved (the level's walls/openings rebuilt) rather than silently dropping the piece; a re-run of the build stage after the conflict is cleared must restore every dropped piece.

A bench drawn in a room typed 'other' (a multi-purpose activity room) is read as a console_table (a low seating/leaning piece that fits an activity room) rather than a bench, which is not an allowed type there.

When one room outline carries two labels and one of them is an open kitchen (AÇIK MUTFAK) inside a living room, the reading must split the outline into a living room and an open-kitchen zone (or keep the kitchen as a sub-zone of the living room) so the kitchen fixtures are placed in the kitchen zone, not the whole living room.
A drawn piece offset by less than 0.25 m from its drawn centre, where the model swap is refused as no_change and no better model exists, is a minor layout drift, not a misread.
A drawn piece offset by less than 0.10 m from its drawn centre is within tolerance and not a misread, even if a slightly better model exists but is unavailable.
A drawn armchair offset by less than 0.15 m where the model swap is not attempted or refused is a minor layout drift, not a misread.
A drawn piece offset by less than 0.15 m where both rotate and swap are refused is a minor layout drift, not a misread.
A drawn piece offset by less than 0.15 m where the swap is refused as asset_unusable is a minor layout drift, not a misread.
A drawn coffee table offset by more than 0.5 m where the move is refused due to overlap with a neighbouring piece is a layout constraint, not a misread; the size mismatch is a model limitation.
A drawn coffee table offset by more than 0.5 m where multiple move attempts are refused due to overlap or drawn_lock is a layout constraint, not a misread.
A drawn nightstand offset by less than 0.20 m is a minor layout drift, not a misread.
A drawn nightstand offset by less than 0.15 m where the swap is refused multiple times is a minor layout drift, not a misread.
A drawn sofa offset by less than 0.35 m is a minor layout drift, not a misread.
A drawn armchair offset by less than 0.35 m where the rotate is refused is a minor layout drift, not a misread.
A bathroom camera that shows only a bare wall or a partially visible fixture should be reframed to show the main fixtures (bathtub, washbasin, toilet) together.
A washbasin that looks like a bare bowl when all alternative models are audit-removed is a model limitation, not a fixable issue.
A chair on a balcony that looks generic when the only better model is refused due to height constraints under a sloped ceiling is a model limitation, not a fixable issue.
A bathroom's program includes a storage piece (tall_cabinet or wall_cabinet); the room_fill stage must place one whenever the bathroom set lacks it, so no bathroom is left with only bare fixtures.

A living room's furniture coverage must reach the furnished-room bar; the decor/dressing stage must add the missing layers (curtains, bedding, styled surfaces, wall art) and the build must apply feature walls and parquet so the room reads as finished, not a bare showroom.

A bedroom's accent wall must carry a feature finish (fluted/panelled wall) in the professional dressing; the decor stage must specify it and the build must apply the feature_walls finish so the room meets the professional bar.

A bed's bedding plan must include a deep duvet that overhangs the free foot side (hem to the floor) and a throw pair; the decor stage must specify the free sides and the build must apply the textiles.bedding_set dressing.
A bed's bedding plan must include a throw across the foot; the decor stage must specify the throw pair's weave and the build must apply the textiles.bedding_set dressing.
A kitchen worktop must carry a few styled props (fruit bowl, kettle, small plant) in the dressing so the counter reads as inhabited, not an empty slab.
A living room's main wall behind the seating must carry wall art or decor to anchor the space; the decor stage must specify the art layer and the build must place it.
Styled surfaces (console and coffee tables) must carry books, a vase or a decorative tray in the dressing so they read as lived-in, not a showroom.
A dining table (indoor or terrace) must carry a table setting (plates, glasses, a centrepiece) in the dressing so it reads as styled, not bare.

A stone-clad wall must use a high-quality, varied stone look (ledger/ashlar with depth) rather than a flat repetitive texture; the build's material assignment must pick a finished stone look for cladding.
An entrance door must be dressed with architectural interest (lighting, a path or steps, surrounding landscaping) so it reads as a proper entrance, not a bare panel.
A desk with a seat must carry a work set (laptop or computer facing the seat) in the dressing so the workspace reads as in use.

The agent stage must not drop a placed furniture piece (e.g. a shoe_cabinet) that the decor stage built; any re-layout must preserve existing pieces or explicitly re-place them, so nothing is silently lost between stages.

The agent stage must not drop a placed furniture piece (e.g. a nightstand) that the decor stage built; any re-layout must preserve existing pieces or explicitly re-place them, so nothing is silently lost between stages.
Sub-parts of a built piece (shelves, cushions, drawers) that the agent drops are not a conservation loss; only the parent piece's disappearance is.
A tall_cabinet drawn in a bathroom that the agent drops must be restored in the next agent round; the bathroom set is incomplete without its storage.
A level that belongs to a specific variant is expected to be absent from the base build; it is built in the variant's own scene.
Decor elements whose host piece is not built must not be silently dropped; the build stage must either build the host or flag the decor for the agent to re-place.
Elements on structural layers (A-BA, A-WALL) are correctly kept as obstacles and not built as furniture.
Furniture symbols drawn on the 'A-TEFRIS' layer must be built as furniture, not skipped; the layer name indicates furniture (Turkish 'tefrishat' = furnishings).
Elements on decor layers (Deko_*) are correctly deferred to the decor stage, not the build stage.
Elements with 60%+ overlap inside a built fixture are correctly treated as parts of that fixture, not separate pieces.

Site areas (parking, terrace, pool) that are drawn in the plan must be built as site elements (paving, grass, water) even if they are exterior; 'not built' is not an acceptable outcome for drawn site areas.
Details inside a kitchen counter (appliance fronts, drawers) are correctly treated as parts of the counter, not separate pieces.
Clusters larger than 4.5 m are correctly identified as groups, not single pieces; the agent stage resolves them.
Elements that both recognition passes classify as not_furniture are correctly kept as obstacles.
Rug outlines (drawn around a table and chairs, with the table and chairs inside) are correctly identified as rug marks, not furniture pieces; the decor stage places them.
Cushion sets that are part of a piece's dressing are built with the piece; their colour-variant dec elements are not separate build targets.
Cushions and pillows that are integral to a furniture model's asset are not separate build targets; they come with the model.
When two pieces of the same type overlap significantly in the same room, the build keeps the larger/clearer one and drops the duplicate; this is correct deduplication, not a loss.
A small piece drawn mostly inside a larger seat (armchair, sofa) is its cushion, not a separate ottoman; the build correctly drops it.
Pieces explicitly removed by an AI action are not built; the build correctly honours the removal.
Large flat outlines around groups of furniture are rugs or zone markers, not furniture pieces; they are handled by the decor rules, not the furniture build.
A large flat outline (roughly 2x2 m or bigger) that encloses two or more placed pieces and has no product of its own is a rug or zone outline, not a furniture piece; it is not built as a piece.
A piece removed by an explicit remove decision is intentionally not built; its absence is not a loss.
The upper end of a stair that arrives at the top level is not rebuilt as a separate piece; the stair is built once between its two floors.
A decor item whose host piece is not built is not built either; its absence follows from the host's.
A bed model that already includes its own made bedding is not additionally dressed with a throw; the model's bedding is kept as is.

A zone label naming a kitchen (e.g. 'AÇIK MUTFAK' / open kitchen) inside a living room marks an open-kitchen zone: the reading stage must classify the enclosed counter as a kitchen zone and keep it as part of the living room's open kitchen, not drop it as an unknown label.
An L-shaped outline with 0.5-1.3 m deep arms in a living room is a corner sofa; the open inner corner is its front.
A single 0.6-0.7 m seat on one side of a coffee table, facing it, is an armchair.
A desk symbol whose footprint includes the chair drawn in front of it is read as the desk at its wall depth plus the chair in front; the chair is kept as a separate piece.

A desk symbol whose drawn footprint is deeper than a desk (roughly 0.9 m or more) is a desk-plus-chair block: build the desk at its real depth against the wall and place the chair in front of it; do not flag the chair as a separate misread.

When a level has no separate kitchen room but the plan draws kitchen fixtures inside a living room, treat it as an open kitchen: keep the fixtures in the living room and do not flag them as misplaced.
A sofa whose front was inferred must be given the direction that looks into the open floor towards its seating partner, not left unoriented.
An armchair whose front was inferred must be given the direction away from its wall or towards its seating partner, not left unoriented.
When a living room has no drawn TV or media wall and no wall 1.5-4 m from the seating axis is clear of windows and doors, do not require a TV place; the room may be a living room without a TV.
When a bedroom has no drawn TV and the wall the bed faces is blocked by furniture (wardrobe, bench, etc.) at every candidate TV position, do not require a TV place; a bedroom does not need a TV.

When the plan labels a room as a terrace or balcony on the top floor and the section draws the roof closed over it, the roof must be cut (or the room treated as an enclosed room) to match the plan; a roof terrace requires an opening in the roof.

When a plan labels a roof terrace and the section draws the roof closed over it, the roof must be cut open over the terrace footprint (a roof terrace) rather than built solid; the door to it stays as the access.

A door whose drawn head would reach over the roof underside at its wall is not usable; the build must provide a dormer (or the architect must confirm the door is not a full-height door) before it is built.
A door whose top is above the roof underside at its wall shows through the roof; the build must clip the door to the roof underside or provide a dormer, and flag the case for review.
Site areas drawn as pools, sunning terraces and parking must be built as site geometry (pool basin + coping + deck/platform + parking slab) when the plan labels them, not dropped as 'no outline'.
Two levels at the same elevation with near-identical room sets are a duplicate read of one floor; the level count must match the section.

A room whose label and drawn furniture (sofa, coffee table, dining table, bookshelf) match a living program must be typed living, not other, even when a twin room on the same level carries the correct type.
A bathroom set is completed to the full set (basin, toilet, bath or shower, tall cabinet) whenever the documents draw a member of the set; a missing member is added, not dropped.

A hall is a circulation space: it is furnished only with a console or bench and a stair, never with a shoe_cabinet or wardrobe, unless the documents explicitly draw an entrance vestibule or storage in that hall.
A balcony or terrace larger than 10 m2 is furnished as a full outdoor room (seating group plus dining table and chairs plus planters), not with a single chair and a table.

Every site area the documents label (pool, sunning terrace, parking, garden) is built as a modelled site element with its outline, paving and water or planting; a labelled site area is never left as bare ground.

A living room with a tv_unit is furnished as a full media wall (tv_unit, sideboard, floor lamp, rug) and a seating group (sofa, armchair, coffee table) with a dining group; a bare wall behind the TV is a fit failure.

A bathroom whose program allows a walk-in shower must be built with a glass walk-in shower (rain head, hand shower on a rail, linear drain), a floating vanity with lit open cubbies and a large backlit mirror, not a bathtub and a plain counter.

Every bathroom must carry one feature wall (a dark fluted WC wall or a stone apron behind and under the vanity), towel bars at the door and at the shower, and towels in one accent colour repeated in two or three places.
Interior doors must be modeled as distinct products with visible panels or profiles, and the entrance door must be visually distinct from interior doors.

Every bathroom render must show the detailed wet-room scheme: an illuminated mirror, a lit open niche or shelf column with styled toiletries, a towel rail, and under-vanity or cove lighting, not a bare tiled wall with a plain mirror.
Interior doors default to open (swung clear of the opening) in renders unless a piece or wall physically stops them; only exterior or privacy doors stay closed.

The bathroom_set group must be able to build the P12 reference (floating fluted vanity with lit cubbies and floor glow, feature panel with matching top, large backlit mirror, walk-in glass shower with rain head, hand shower on rail and linear drain, towel shelf, two-cluster counter) when the room's family allows it, instead of only a basic washbasin/toilet/cabinet/shower set.

The bathroom build must include the P13 reference: one feature wall (dark fluted WC wall or stone apron behind/under the vanity), a mirror shaped and framed by the family, towel bars at the door and at the shower, and towels in one accent colour repeated in two or three places.

An interior view that includes a door to a room worth showing must frame that door open with the room beyond lit and furnished; a view whose only door is closed should be re-aimed to show the room's own furnished pieces instead.

Interior doors must stand open by default (leaf turned against its swing side); a render that shows an interior door fully closed is a camera/door-state error to be corrected by re-aiming the view or opening the leaf.
Every bathroom must have at least one window or a light well to provide daylight and ventilation, unless it is a wet room with a mechanical ventilation system explicitly shown in the documents.

Every bathroom render must carry the reference detail set: an illuminated mirror, a lit open niche or shelf with toiletries, a towel rail, a paper holder and large-format wall tiles, not a bare wall with a plain framed mirror.

Interior doors render open by default wherever the swing is unobstructed, and door finishes vary by family (glazed divided-lite where the plan calls for it) rather than all being identical closed slabs.

A bathroom whose family allows the P12 reference must be furnished to that reference (floating vanity, feature panel, backlit mirror, walk-in shower with glass, rain head, linear drain, towel shelf) rather than a basic set, when its area and layout permit it.

A bathroom whose family allows the P13 reference must include one feature wall, a family-shaped framed mirror, towel bars at the door and shower, and towels in one accent colour repeated in two or three places.
